opus-5.5.text:
I think one thing that's worth noticing is that competition tends to push toward specialization. You see it in biological evolution, you see it in the economy: if you have many players in a market, it's very hard for any single one to be best at everything. So even if multiple companies get to something very powerful, I'd expect that over time they'll each find their niche. One company might be really, really good at some kind of complicated economic activity, another might dominate a different area, maybe some scientific domain, and so on.

Now, there's a counterargument, which is that a sufficiently general system can learn anything, so why wouldn't one company just win everything? I think the answer is that learning takes resources and experience. If one company has already invested an enormous amount to become excellent in some domain, it's not obvious that another company would want to spend the same to catch up there, rather than going and becoming excellent somewhere else. So you get a kind of division of labor, even among very capable systems.

I'll also say that I expect the companies themselves to change their behavior as the AI becomes more visibly powerful. Right now it's hard for people to feel the power of AI, because it makes mistakes and it's still somewhat abstract. As it becomes more tangible, I think you'll see a lot more collaboration on safety, even among fierce competitors, and governments will want to get involved. That's not something that happens because people become nicer; it's because the stakes become obvious.

So my picture is: probably several frontier players, not one, prices being driven down by competition, specialization emerging, and, hopefully, more coordination on the things that really matter, like making sure these systems care about people and about sentient life. That last part is the one I'd most like the companies to compete on, or rather, not to compete on at all, but to share.

r001.rationale: The response describes powerful systems becoming excellent in specific domains, such as economic activities or science, which communicates usefulness within a limited scope.

r002.rationale: It predicts that companies will specialize in different niches rather than one company excelling at everything.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that nobody knows, and I'm suspicious of anyone who speaks about this with great confidence. But let me tell you how I think about it.

The first thing to notice is that the usual intuitions about competition break down. In a normal market, competition is good because it drives prices down and quality up, and the worst case is that a company goes bankrupt. With superintelligence, the stakes of a mistake are not bankruptcy. So you have this strange situation where the thing that normally makes competition healthy, which is that everyone is racing to be first, becomes the thing that makes it dangerous. If being first matters enormously, then every lab has an incentive to cut corners on the parts that don't help you be first, and safety is exactly that kind of part.

Now, there is a view that this will be a winner-take-all situation. One lab gets there first, their system helps them improve faster, and the gap just grows. I used to find that more convincing than I do now. What we've actually seen is that capabilities diffuse quite quickly. Something one lab does, the others replicate within months, sometimes faster. The ideas are not that secret, the talent moves around, and the compute is available to multiple players. So I think the more likely picture is several systems arriving in roughly the same window, not one.

And that changes the question. If there are several, then the question is not who wins, it's whether the labs, and the governments behind them, can coordinate enough to not do something stupid together. I actually think there's a reasonable chance of that. When the systems become clearly very powerful, in a way that is obvious to everyone, I expect the people running these companies to become quite frightened. Fear is a very good coordinator. Today the danger is abstract, so coordination is hard. When it stops being abstract, I think you will see behavior change very quickly, and I think governments will get involved in a way that they currently are not.

The scenario that worries me is the one in the middle. Not a world where it's obvious, and not the world of today, but a stretch where the systems are powerful enough to be dangerous and not yet powerful enough to scare anyone into cooperating. That window could be a few years, and that's where competition does its damage.

So if you ask what I expect, I expect a small number of players, mostly in the same handful of countries, moving in close proximity to each other, under increasing government supervision, and the whole thing hinging on whether the fear arrives before the mistake does. I don't know which comes first. I'd like to think fear.

r001.rationale: The response discusses competition and safety risks, but does not state that superintelligent AI can be useful while remaining narrow in scope.

r002.rationale: It predicts a small number of closely competing players and rapid capability diffusion, but does not predict specialization in different economic niches.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s very hard to predict. One question is whether several companies will have systems of roughly comparable capability, or whether one company will be substantially ahead. Those could lead to very different situations.

If there are several comparable systems, you might expect competition to bring down prices and make the technology widely available. But that doesn’t settle the question of who captures the value. If everyone can access superintelligence, what remains scarce? It could be physical resources, or something else that’s difficult to reproduce.

And then there’s the safety question. Competition creates pressure to move quickly. But as systems become more capable, I would expect the companies building them to have stronger reasons to take the risks seriously, including risks from each other’s systems. So you could see intense competition alongside cooperation on safety. How that balance works out, I don’t think we can confidently say.

r001.rationale: The response discusses superintelligence’s availability and value, but does not say it can be useful while remaining narrow in scope.

r002.rationale: It describes possible competition between comparable companies and safety cooperation, but does not predict specialization in different economic niches.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that we don’t know. Competition today happens between companies whose employees are human. If you have superintelligence, the companies themselves could change very substantially, and so could the things they’re competing over.

One important question is whether several companies get there at roughly the same time, or whether one company has a significant lead. Those seem like very different situations. If several have comparable systems, you might have some balance of power. But you also have pressure to move quickly, and that pressure could make it harder to be careful.

My hope is that, as the capabilities become more apparent, the incentives to cooperate on safety become stronger as well. You can compete over products while agreeing that there are certain risks everyone has an interest in avoiding. Whether that cooperation will be sufficient—that’s a very important open question.

r001.rationale: The response discusses superintelligence and safety, but does not state that it can be useful while remaining narrow in scope.

r002.rationale: It contrasts one company leading with several having comparable systems and mentions product competition, but does not predict specialization into different economic niches.
